title: Feistel Network
body:
The construction that made block ciphers practical, and the architecture of DES. Its trick is
worth more than the cipher built on it: **it turns any function at all into an invertible one.**

## The round

Split the block in half. Each round takes $(L_i, R_i)$ to

$$L_{i+1} = R_i, \qquad R_{i+1} = L_i \oplus F(R_i, k_i)$$

where $F$ is the *round function* and $k_i$ is a per-round subkey derived from the key.

Now invert it. Given $(L_{i+1}, R_{i+1})$ you know $R_i = L_{i+1}$, so you can recompute
$F(R_i, k_i)$ and XOR it back off:

$$R_i = L_{i+1}, \qquad L_i = R_{i+1} \oplus F(L_{i+1}, k_i)$$

**$F$ is never inverted.** It does not have to be injective, or even interesting; the XOR does all
the invertibility and $F$ is free to be as messy and non-linear as you like. That is the whole
insight, and the consequence is the one implementers care about: **decryption is the same circuit
as encryption with the subkeys fed in reverse order**, so a hardware implementation costs one
datapath rather than two. Compare [[AES]], which is not a Feistel cipher and does need separate
inverse operations for each of its steps.

```
encryption:  k1 k2 k3 ... k16
decryption:  k16 ... k3 k2 k1     same hardware
```

## DES

The Data Encryption Standard, 1977, 16 Feistel rounds on a 64-bit block with a 56-bit key. Each
round function expands the 32-bit half to 48 bits, XORs the subkey, pushes the result through eight
**S-boxes**, and permutes the output with a **P-box**:

| Component | Provides | Shannon's name |
|---|---|---|
| S-box | non-linear 6-bit-in, 4-bit-out lookup | confusion |
| P-box | fixed bit permutation | diffusion |
| 16 rounds | avalanche across the whole block | both |

The S-boxes are the only non-linear part and therefore the only thing standing between DES and
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]. Their contents looked arbitrary in 1977 and were criticised as a possible
backdoor; when **differential cryptanalysis** was published in 1990 the S-boxes turned out to be
specifically hardened against it, which the designers had known about and not said. The P-box is a
[[Transposition Cipher]] on bits, doing at the bit level what the classical block did at the letter
level.

**DES is dead, and it died of key length.** 56 bits is $7.2 \times 10^{16}$ keys, brute-forced in
public in 1998 in 56 hours by purpose-built hardware. No structural weakness was needed. That is
the [[Cryptanalysis|brute-force baseline]] catching up with a fixed parameter, and it is why
[[AES]] starts at 128 bits.

**3DES** patched it by encrypting three times with two or three keys ($E_{k_1}D_{k_2}E_{k_3}$),
giving about 112 bits of effective security at three times the cost. Double DES is *not* worth
doing: the **meet-in-the-middle attack** breaks it at roughly $2^{57}$ work rather than $2^{112}$,
by encrypting the known plaintext under every $k_1$, decrypting the ciphertext under every $k_2$,
and looking for a match in a table. It is [[Hashing|hash table]] lookup used as an attack, and
trading memory for time is a general enough move that it is worth remembering outside this course.

## What to take from it

- Feistel is a **generic construction**, not a cipher. Blowfish, Twofish, and Camellia all use it.
- The round function need not be invertible, which is why it can be built out of table lookups.
- Security comes from **round count**: a 3-round Feistel is distinguishable from random, a 4-round
  one is provably secure against chosen-plaintext attack given random round functions (Luby-Rackoff),
  and real designs use 16 for margin.
- Block ciphers only encrypt one block. Anything longer needs a [[Modes of Operation|mode]].
